newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian corruption row senator silent on future.
newsitem.headline: Australian corruption row senator silent on future.

text.p: A key Australian independent senator whose support is crucial to government reforms on Sunday rejected mounting calls to quit an influential upper house post while police investigate corruption allegations.
Mal Colston, who is being treated at a Brisbane hospital for a lung infection, issued a statement saying he would not make any decisions about his political future while he was ill.
But in a newspaper interview published on Sunday, he did rule out quitting the Senate.
"I am not going to resign from the Senate," Colston was quoted by The Sunday Telegraph as saying. The senator has denied breaking any laws.
Senate president Margaret Reid urged Colston to stand aside as her deputy president before the upper house resumes sittings on May 6.
"I hope that he'll stand down from the deputy presidency. That is something that he should do," said Reid, who cut short an overseas trip because of the scandal.
"From one point of view you would say the Senate may have been misled quite grievously, and that is something from the Senate's point that is very serious," she said in a television interview.
Reid said she expected the Senate to dump Colston as deputy if he refused to stand aside, but ruled out Labor opposition demands to recall the chamber early.
Colston repaid almost A$7,000 (US$5,500) last month after a Senate inquiry found he had wrongly claimed travel allowances, but he blamed the incident on sloppy book-keeping.

Prime Minister John Howard last week called in police to investigate allegations of benefits abuse and withdrew government support for Colston's deputy presidency after a former Colston staffer recanted an earlier statement taking blame for the book-keeping.

Howard's year-old conservative administration does not have a majority in the Senate. It relies on the support of Colston, who defected from Labor last year to sit as an independent, and another independent to pass key measures, including budget cuts.
If Colston leaves the Senate, he would be replaced by a Labor Party member because he was elected as a Labor senator.
Such a move would alter the balance of power in the Senate, although Labor would still be short of a majority.
But it would cast doubt over the government's ability to pass legislation through the upper house, including the 1997/98 budget due to be announced on May 13.
